power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Evaluating Alibis Based on Schematic (In)consistencies
table.research_questions:
# Expectation (Routine for Past Behaviors)


## Research Question 1

Context: Cardenas, Crozier, & Strange (2020) asked participants to report on their typical routines (if any) for 112 (16 hours x 7 days) time periods. Participants rated the typicality of each of these routines on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very atypical; 7 = very typical).

What percentage of sampled time periods do people think they have routines for (i.e., rate as highly typical)?


# Reality (Actual Behavior)

## Research Question 2
Context: Cardenas, Crozier, & Strange (2020) conducted experience-sampling over two weeks and collected information from people about up to 56 events/behaviors (4 times per day x 14 days).

Of the events that people rate as highly typical, what % of events were people engaged in a typical behavior consistent with their routine vs. atypical behaviors inconsistent with their routine?

## Research Question 3

How well do ratings of expected typicality of behaviors predict whether sampled events were typical (behavior consistent with routine) (vs. atypical)?

# Recall of Actual Behavior

## Research Question 4
Cardenas, Crozier, & Strange (2020) selected 4 of the up to 56 events of actual behavior sampled to create participant-specific memory tests. For 2 of the 4 events participants' Actual Behavior was consistent with their expected routine. For 2 of the 4 events participants' Actual Behavior was inconsistent with their expected routine. For more information on how events were chosen see Cardenas et al.

How well do ratings of expected typicality of behaviors predict accuracy of recall for typical vs. atypical events? # RQ 1: We expect the proportion to be high. However, it should be noted that the first author is familiar with this dataset. They have not performed summary statistics but were involved in overseeing the initial coding that produced the dataset and cannot discount that the source of this prediction may be data-driven.

# RQ2: We expect the proportion here to be low. However, it should be noted that the first author is familiar with this dataset. They have not performed summary statistics but were involved in overseeing the initial coding that produced the dataset and cannot discount that the source of this prediction may be data-driven.

#RQ3: Given the high proportion of participants in Cardenas et al. that relied on their schemas to inform their alibis for schema-inconsistent events, we expect that expectations about their routines will not strongly predict whether participants were engaged in those routines.

#RQ4: Cardenas et al. report the influence of typicality as a covariate. The current analysis will isolate the effect of typicality. In line with above predictions, we expect that people's estimates of typicality will not be diagnostic of accuracy of recall.

The goal of the current pre-registration is to pre-register the data wrangling and analysis plan.

table.unit_of_analysis: Not all participants completes all phases of the studies described in Cardenas et al. We will use data available at each phase, such that responses to expectations about routine events (T1) will correspond to a larger sample size than responses to memory test (T3). Missing data for T2 responses were indicated in the original coding scheme. We will assess what proportion of T2 (actual behaviors) were missing and what proportion corresponds to each participant and report these, as well as potential causes identified by the authors in their original documentation (e.g., participants were asked to not report their T2 whereabouts if they were engaged in sensitive or illegal activities, or if more than an hour had elapsed since the time of receipt of query).
table.missing_data_handling:
Missing data will be removed only at the level of the smallest unit of data (e.g., reporting for a specific time period or specific detail - person, setting, or action). 

The manuscript describes 152 participants (80 in Study 1, and 72 in Study 2) as having completed Phase 1 (T1 - Expected Routines). Therefore, we expect that for each of these individuals we will obtain over 51,000 data points (3 detail types (setting, action, person) * 7 days*16 time periods between 7 am and 11 pm). 

For T2 (Reporting of Actual Behaviors), 140 participants completed reporting of their actual behaviors. The amount of queries varied by recruitment batch, such that participants received between 30 and 56 times queries each. Thus, we expect between 12,600 and 23520 data points for each participant (when broken down my setting, action, person detail); or information about between 4200 and 7840 events in total. 

For T3 (Recall of Actual Behaviors), there are 507 events (279 and 228 across the two studies).
table.statistical_outliers: We do not anticipate removal of any outliers at this time. However, should this be required we will follow our previous protocol of removing those values outside the interval formed by the median plus or minus 3 median absolute values  (Leys et al. 2013).
table.prior_publication_dissemination:

table.statistical_tests:
We are primarily using this dataset for exploratory purposes and to report descriptive information pertaining to our research questions.

For Hypothesis 3, we will test mixed effects models that account for variance resulting from participant, event type (discrete time period, total 112; time of day, total 3; week day, total 7), and batch. Here will will assess the influence of self-reported Typicality on the actual consistency between participants' expectations and behaviors (T1T2_consistency).

For Hypothesis 4, we will also test a mixed effects models that account for variance resulting from participant, study, and memory elicitation technique. Here will will assess the influence of self-reported Typicality on the consistency between participants' behaviors and their recalled behaviors (TAST2T3). 

The code we will use for all these analyses can be found at https://osf.io/y3nec.
table.statistical_power: Given the large dataset, we do not expect any power issues.
table.inference_criteria: We will conclude that a regression analysis supports our hypothesis if the p-value is smaller than .01.
table.q25: Should the model fail to converge we will attempt to use different optimizers, if that does not work we will log-transform the variable.
table.exploratory_analyses: As an exploratory analysis, we will assess whether variations in reported typicality or consistency between expectations and routine bheaviors result from time of day, week day, or time period differences.

What percentage of sampled time periods do people think they have routines for (i.e., rate as highly typical)?


# Reality (Actual Behavior)

## Research Question 2
Context: Cardenas, Crozier, & Strange (2020) conducted experience-sampling over two weeks and collected information from people about up to 56 events/behaviors (4 times per day x 14 days).

Of the events that people rate as highly typical, what % of events were people engaged in a typical behavior consistent with their routine vs. atypical behaviors inconsistent with their routine?

# Recall of Actual Behavior

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p > .05", Text = "The slope-based TOST was inconclusive, b = 0.08, SE = 0.05, p > .05."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. table.text: As hypothesized, sampled occasions expected to be more typical showed significantly greater consistency, b = 0.09, SE = 0.02, t(1359.77) = 5.29, p < .001; each one-point increase in expected typicality predicted a modest increase of .09 in matching person, action, or setting domain information on the 0 to 3 expectation-behavior consistency scale.

"Thank you for participating in this study! Dr. Stephanie A. Cardenas, a Visiting Assistant Professor of Psychology at Williams College, and Destiny J. Crisp, a senior honors thesis student, designed this study. We appreciate your time and dedication to this research. The study you just completed is interested in investigating the effects of context and role on memory and alibi believability. Despite a criminal justice system that asserts ‘innocent till proven guilty,’ preliminary evidence demonstrates that specific contexts, such as a criminal trial, may function as guilt-presumptive contexts (Sommers & Douglass, 2007; Crozier et al., 2019). In past research, participants have been tasked with imagining themselves as various legal stakeholders in the criminal justice process, such as police detectives and jurors. However, no prior work has explicitly examined the impact of adopting a specific role. Thus, the present study wished to explore how the context in which an alibi is presented and a participant’s assigned role influence alibi believability and memory recall. We hypothesize that certain contexts and roles may result in biased memory and perceptions of the burglary case. Accordingly, the current research will provide critical information on the bias-related mechanisms that influence how an individual and their alibi are evaluated. We appreciate your contribution to this critical research. If you have any additional questions, comments, or concerns, please contact psy.cognition.lab@gmail.com.",

#### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Registration's Source Project Is Closed

1 OSF source project is closed. The files metacheck lists below were not read from it — they were retrieved from the OSF registration's own copy, which is separate from and unaffected by the project's access setting. Nothing is currently lost, but this is still worth fixing: a closed source project means the files only survive for as long as the registration's copy does, and anyone who follows the project link itself (rather than the registration) will find it inaccessible.

- **https://osf.io/p3qs9** is closed; its files were retrieved from the OSF registration https://osf.io/v39m4.

Consider making the source project openly available.

#### Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository's files are grouped: the repository separates out a study (ex3) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 502 columns across 12 data files.
#### Issues Identified

23 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were recruited for a study ostensibly on sleep and emotional well-being.
Study 1 participants completed Time 3 remotely through Qualtrics, whereas Study 2 participants completed Time 3 during a laboratory interview.
In Study 2 only, at Time 4, 58 participants provided a second set of 218 retrospective reports about the same occasions from Time 3.
Participants were ethnically diverse with 55 identifying as Hispanic or Latina/o, 52 as White, 30 as Black or African American, 22 as Asian, 5 as Other.
Participants were encouraged to consult their planners to increase the accuracy of their reported routines.
Next, 144 participants completed an experience-sampling phase lasting 10 to 14 days.
For each message, participants were prompted to respond with 1) who they were with, 2) what they were doing, and 3) where they were, along with filler items about their current emotional state.
To prevent rehearsal of their responses, participants were instructed to avoid discussing their messages and to delete them.
On average, each participant provided 28.5 concurrent reports (SD = 8.27, range = 7-51).

Finally, just over a week later (M = 7.94 days, SD = 3.55: range: 1.77-35), 134 participants completed a personalized free-recall memory test asking them to recall their behavior during four occasions sampled at Time 2.
Participants were asked to imagine themselves as suspects in a criminal investigation and that the accuracy of their memory reports would serve as alibis supporting their innocence.
For two of four sampled occasions, participants were cued only by the target one-hour window; for the other two sampled occasions, recall was elicited via a mental reinstatement of context procedure.
In total, participants provided 507 retrospective reports: 111 participants provided four reports, 17 provided three, and six provided two; none provided only one.
Only Study 2 participants participated in Time 4 tasks.
Participants provided a total of 218 additional retrospective reports: 49 participants provided four reports, four provided three, and five provided two; none provided only one.
Higher scores indicated greater occasion-level consistency between what participants had actually been doing and what they retrospectively reported doing.

Concurrent reports at Time 2 were excluded if during Time 1 prospective reporting, the participant had indicated no routine or, less commonly, a partial routine, as no measure of expectation-behavior consistency could be calculated (k = 348 observations).
Descriptively, participants were less consistent about what they would be doing than who or where they would be with.
Fourth, some sampled occasions lacked usable concurrent reports at Time 2, raising concern that report availability may have depended on what participants were doing.
However, when we reviewed all available Time 1 data, we found that 207, not 152, participants had consented and provided any Time 1 responses (i.e., completed one or more of the 112 time periods).

We suspect that, by "completed," Cárdenas et al. meant that a participant had completed all 112 time periods and provided contact information, primarily a phone number, which was necessary for the Phase 2 experience sampling.
We cannot be completely certain why Cárdenas et al. reported that 152 rather than 151 participants completed Time 1.
It is possible that 152 participants provided contact information and that this criterion determined who Cárdenas et al. counted as having completed Time 1.
• 151 participants provided demographic information.
• The source study reported that 152 participants completed Time 1; one additional participant may have provided contact information but not demographic information.
In a few cases, participants were allowed to join an ongoing experience-sampling phase a day or two late.
Four reports from one participant were ineligible due to receiving the wrong survey link.
Four reports from one participant were never submitted.
Ten reports from six participants were unavailable due to the same reason they had missing Time 3 recall accuracy scores.
Four reports from four participants were missing due to other technical issues with their personalized survey that affected only one time period.
All participants had some data from time periods excluded.
Participants were ethnically diverse: Among the 142 who provided ethnicity data, 53 identified as Hispanic or Latino/a, 49 as White, 28 as Black or African American, 19 as Asian, and 5 as Other.
At Time 3 (in Study 1) or Time 4 (in Study 2), participants were asked to rate how often they looked at the texts they sent us, despite instructions to delete their messages after sending them to us.
Data pertaining to 71 Study 1 participants and 51 Study 2 participants are available.
The remaining 52 participants provided partial prospective reports, most often discontinuing after completing the Monday time periods (36 of 52 participants).

These comparisons likely somewhat overestimate non-completers' expected routines because task progress was confounded with day of week: participants completed the planner in Monday-to-Sunday order, and Monday-Thursday periods tended to receive slightly higher typicality ratings than Friday-Sunday periods (see S19).

Among the 764 of 3,510 experience-sampled events that participants had rated as low to moderately typical (1 to 5) at Time 1, even fewer events occurred as expected than among events rated as highly typical.
1 It did in 43.7% of cases (87 of 199), indicating that even when participants were wrong, they still reproduced an expectationconsistent detail nearly half the time.
In Study 2, 16 participants indicated being community members recruited via Craigslist, whereas 44 were recruited via undergraduates recruited via flyers posted on college campuses.
Second, only Study 2 participants completed the Time 4 commonness rating.
Only Study 2 participants completed Time 4 measures.
Planner UseAt Time 3 (in Study 1) or Time 4 (in Study 2), participants were asked "How often do you use a planner in your daily life to organize your schedule?"
Levels containing fewer than 6 participants were omitted.

#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 18 scripts: 2 ran without error, 12 errored, 0 timed out, 2 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 2 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `004-01-reproducible-supplemental-materials-analyses.Rmd` (time_2_scheduled_ema_times.csv, time_2_concurrent_reports_3510.csv). text.text: People report as memories not only what they retrieve, but what seems plausible.
Routine knowledge may inform plausibility judgments and support accurate reconstruction when behavior follows an expected routine.
But how often does behavior match those routine expectations?
We conducted preregistered analyses of previously collected longitudinal data from student and community samples (N = 207;Cárdenas et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We conducted preregistered analyses of previously collected longitudinal data from student and community samples (N = 207;<ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cárdenas et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We compared expected routines for 18,736 day-and-hour periods-e.g., Tuesdays, 1-2 PM-with 3,510 one-time experience-sampled occasions and 725 retrospective reports.
Participants expected complete routines during 92.83% of waking-hour periods, but behavior matched at least two of three expected domains on only 44.39% of occasions expected to be highly typical.
Expected typicality did not reliably predict recall accuracy.
Exploratorily, higher expected typicality predicted greater schema reliance: retrospective reports reproduced expectations that had not matched sampled behavior.
Routine knowledge may provide a less reliable basis for reconstruction than participants' confidence in their routines suggests.
People are sometimes asked to account for an ordinary moment in their pasts.
A romantic partner may ask where the other was one evening, while a doctor may ask what a patient was doing when symptoms began.
A detective may ask a suspect or corroborator for an alibi at a particular time.

Errors in autobiographical recall can contribute to interpersonal strain (Ray et al., 2019), clinical errors (Redelmeier et al., 2001), and wrongful convictions when inaccurate alibis appear deceptive (Crozier et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Errors in autobiographical recall can contribute to interpersonal strain <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Ray et al., 2019)</ref>, clinical errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Redelmeier et al., 2001)</ref>, and wrongful convictions when inaccurate alibis appear deceptive <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crozier et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Yet mundane everyday moments may not be encoded with later retrieval in mind (Brewer, 1988), leaving people to reconstruct what likely happened from expectations about what usually happens at that time (Barclay, 1986; Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000).
text.formatted: Yet mundane everyday moments may not be encoded with later retrieval in mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brewer, 1988)</ref>, leaving people to reconstruct what likely happened from expectations about what usually happens at that time <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Barclay, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: To evaluate this strategy, we use naturalistic experience sampling to examine whether time-specific routine expectations-expectations about what usually happens during recurring day-and-hour time periods (e.g., Tuesdays, 1-2 PM)-match sampled behavior and inform later reconstruction.
People may base reconstruction on schemas, which represent common features of repeated experiences (Bartlett, 1932; Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014).
text.formatted: People may base reconstruction on schemas, which represent common features of repeated experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bartlett, 1932;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In everyday life, people may draw on generalized knowledge of repeated personal experiences and familiar event scripts to form expectations about where they are usually found, what they usually do, with whom, and, critically, at what specific times (Brewer, 1986; Schank & Abelson, 1977).
text.formatted: In everyday life, people may draw on generalized knowledge of repeated personal experiences and familiar event scripts to form expectations about where they are usually found, what they usually do, with whom, and, critically, at what specific times <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Brewer, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Schank & Abelson, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: By providing a framework for what is expected, schemas guide how people perceive, remember, and interpret information (Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023).
text.formatted: By providing a framework for what is expected, schemas guide how people perceive, remember, and interpret information <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, research suggests that people perceive much of everyday behavior as habitual and view routines as a pervasive feature of daily life (Rebar et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Indeed, research suggests that people perceive much of everyday behavior as habitual and view routines as a pervasive feature of daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Rebar et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For example, recent work found that adults estimated that most of their own and others' waking hours followed routines that "repeated with some degree of regularity usually at approximately the same days and times with few exceptions" (Mdn = 70%, SD = 18.41; Thy et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, recent work found that adults estimated that most of their own and others' waking hours followed routines that "repeated with some degree of regularity usually at approximately the same days and times with few exceptions" (Mdn = 70%, SD = 18.41; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Thy et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, prior work has not examined how often people expect routines during particular day-and-hour periods or mapped those expectations to reality.

If people hold a strong perception of regularity for most waking hours, and such perceptions are accurate, knowledge about one's routines may provide an efficient basis for inferring what likely happened when episodic memory is weak or unavailable.

Conversely, schema-based inference is also risky because it can lead people to substitute expectation for actual experience (Brewer & Treyens, 1981; Lampinen et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 1985; Neuschatz et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Conversely, schema-based inference is also risky because it can lead people to substitute expectation for actual experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brewer & Treyens, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lampinen et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Nakamura et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Neuschatz et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: When what usually happens fails to happen at the expected time, or fails to happen altogether, reconstructions may produce reports that are consistent with the schema for that time period rather than with what actually occurred (Leins & Charman, 2016).
text.formatted: When what usually happens fails to happen at the expected time, or fails to happen altogether, reconstructions may produce reports that are consistent with the schema for that time period rather than with what actually occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Leins & Charman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This risk may be especially likely for repeated behaviors, because memory often preserves the general pattern of recurring events better than the details that distinguish one occurrence from another (Dilevski et al., 2022; Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023).
text.formatted: This risk may be especially likely for repeated behaviors, because memory often preserves the general pattern of recurring events better than the details that distinguish one occurrence from another <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dilevski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Timespecific cues do not always solve this problem, because ordinary events are often weakly encoded with respect to when they occurred (Friedman, 1993; Thompson et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Timespecific cues do not always solve this problem, because ordinary events are often weakly encoded with respect to when they occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Friedman, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Thompson et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: When direct recollection is weak, memory reports depend not only on what people retrieve, but also on how they evaluate candidate events before deciding whether to report them (Koriat & Goldsmith, 1996).
text.formatted: When direct recollection is weak, memory reports depend not only on what people retrieve, but also on how they evaluate candidate events before deciding whether to report them <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Koriat & Goldsmith, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Metacognitive models of autobiographical belief suggest that this evaluative process draws on inferential cues-including perceived event prevalence, plausibility, and script knowledge (Mazzoni & Hanczakowski, 2011; Mazzoni & Kirsch, 2002; Scoboria et al., 2014; Scoboria et al., 2006; Scoboria et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Metacognitive models of autobiographical belief suggest that this evaluative process draws on inferential cues-including perceived event prevalence, plausibility, and script knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Mazzoni & Hanczakowski, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Mazzoni & Kirsch, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Scoboria et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Scoboria et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Scoboria et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: If beliefs about the frequency and stability of one's routines are strong, they may make routine-consistent events seem especially plausible.
Yet if those beliefs are poorly calibrated to reality, routine-based reconstruction may systematically replace actual behavior with expected behavior.
This issue has significant implications for the high-stakes context of criminal investigations (Charman & Shambaugh, 2022).
text.formatted: This issue has significant implications for the high-stakes context of criminal investigations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Charman & Shambaugh, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Innocent suspects are often asked to account for a specific past moment that, given their lack of involvement with the crime, was likely ordinary and therefore unlikely to have been encoded in a way that would support its retrieval (Crozier et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Innocent suspects are often asked to account for a specific past moment that, given their lack of involvement with the crime, was likely ordinary and therefore unlikely to have been encoded in a way that would support its retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crozier et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Laboratory-based experiments show that innocent suspects often rely on schematic knowledge of their routines to generate alibis (Eastwood et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Laboratory-based experiments show that innocent suspects often rely on schematic knowledge of their routines to generate alibis <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Eastwood et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This reliance is sometimes helpful: Alibis for schema-consistent occasions tend to be more accurate than alibis for schema-inconsistent occasions (Leins & Charman, 2016).
text.formatted: This reliance is sometimes helpful: Alibis for schema-consistent occasions tend to be more accurate than alibis for schema-inconsistent occasions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Leins & Charman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, schemas may not always cue actual episodic memories.

In Cárdenas et al. (2021), alibis for schema-consistent occasions did not reliably show stronger subjective markers of recollective experience, such as vividness, confidence, or remember/know judgments.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cárdenas et al. (2021)</ref>, alibis for schema-consistent occasions did not reliably show stronger subjective markers of recollective experience, such as vividness, confidence, or remember/know judgments.

text.text: Nor were these markers reliably associated with recall accuracy.
Accuracy likewise did not vary with the delay between event occurrence and recall, despite substantial evidence linking longer delays with poorer recall accuracy (Murre & Dros, 2015).
text.formatted: Accuracy likewise did not vary with the delay between event occurrence and recall, despite substantial evidence linking longer delays with poorer recall accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Murre & Dros, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These results suggest that some schema-consistent alibis may reflect routine knowledge rather than direct memory for the target event.

Critically, reliance on routine knowledge can also backfire, leading people to report expected behaviors when they instead engaged in unexpected behaviors (Cárdenas et al., 2021; Eastwood et al., 2021; Leins & Charman, 2016).
text.formatted: Critically, reliance on routine knowledge can also backfire, leading people to report expected behaviors when they instead engaged in unexpected behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cárdenas et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwood et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Leins & Charman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This work shows that people rely on routine knowledge when reconstructing the past, but it says much less about whether people's expectations about their routines are often accurate enough to justify that use, or about how often routine-consistent versus routine-inconsistent situations occur in the first place.
Using previously unreported longitudinal data collected by Cárdenas and colleagues (2021), we link prospective, concurrent, and retrospective reports to investigate three questions.
text.formatted: Using previously unreported longitudinal data collected by <ref type="bibr">Cárdenas and colleagues (2021)</ref>, we link prospective, concurrent, and retrospective reports to investigate three questions.

text.text: First, how often do people expect routines for particular day-and-hour periods?
Second, when people expect a day-and-hour period to be highly routine, how often does their behavior on a subsequently sampled occasion align with that expectation?
Third, does higher expected typicality predict the accuracy of later reports about those sampled occasions?
An expected routine comprises the person, action, and setting details anticipated to recur during that period.
A sampled occasion is one real-time instance of that period.
We predicted that time-specific routine expectations would be common but often fail to match sampled occasions.
We further predicted that expected typicality would weakly predict how closely sampled behavior matched expected routines, but not recall accuracy.

text.text: We report novel analyses of a newly wrangled dataset drawn from two closely related longitudinal studies conducted by Cárdenas and colleagues (2021).
text.formatted: We report novel analyses of a newly wrangled dataset drawn from two closely related longitudinal studies conducted by <ref type="bibr">Cárdenas and colleagues (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Study 1 collected data from November 15, 2017 (Time 1) through February 26, 2018 (Time 3).
Study 2 collected data from March 28, 2018 (Time 1) through May 29, 2018 (Time 4); the researchers avoided holidays during Time 2 sampling.
Both studies followed similar procedures and used the same measures through Time 3, as such we pooled all available observations across studies.
Participants were recruited for a study ostensibly on sleep and emotional well-being.
At Time 1, they reported expected routines for recurring time periods via Qualtrics survey.
At Time 2, they reported their concurrent behavior during an approximately 10-day experience sampling phase via textmessaging.
At Time 3, they retrospectively reported their behavior during four Time 2 sampled occasions.
Study 1 participants completed Time 3 remotely through Qualtrics, whereas Study 2 participants completed Time 3 during a laboratory interview.
Study 2 added a second retrospective report at Time 4.

Both studies relied on convenience samples of undergraduate students from an urban commuter college in the northeastern United States; however, to further increase demographic diversity, Study 2 broadened recruitment to include local community members.
Compensation of up to $50 was prorated based on completion of each study phase.
Across source studies, at Time 1, 207 participants (Study 1: n = 99, Study 2: n = 108) provided 18,736 prospective reports of expected routines for time periods.

This exceeded the 152-sample size we anticipated in our preregistration because the available data included participants who provided at least one Time 1 response, not only those classified by Cárdenas et al. (2021) as completing Time 1 (Supplemental Material S1).
text.formatted: This exceeded the 152-sample size we anticipated in our preregistration because the available data included participants who provided at least one Time 1 response, not only those classified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cárdenas et al. (2021)</ref> as completing Time 1 (Supplemental Material S1).

text.text: Retaining these participants was nevertheless consistent with our preregistered plan to use all data available at each phase (Supplemental Material S1).
At Time 2, 144 participants (Study 1: n = 76, Study 2: n = 68) reported their behavior on 3,510 concurrently sampled occasions.
At Time 3, 134 (Study 1: n = 74, Study 2: n = 60) provided 507 retrospective reports about selected sampled occasions.
In Study 2 only, at Time 4, 58 participants provided a second set of 218 retrospective reports about the same occasions from Time 3.
See Figure 1.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Differences in sample size reflect attrition across study phases.
For retention, demographic, and sample-type analyses, see Supplemental Materials S2-S4.

The current study adds previously unreported data from Time 1 and Time 2, observations from an additional 73 participants (Study 1: n = 25; Study 2: n = 48) who had been excluded from Cárdenas et al. (2021) for not providing Time 3 data, and novel analyses documenting associations across time points.

(2021)</ref> for not providing Time 3 data, and novel analyses documenting associations across time points.

text.text: As preregistered, we adopted a more conservative alpha level of .01 for null-hypothesis significance testing to account for the anticipated large size of the dataset.

Among participants who provided demographic data (n = 151 of 207), ages ranged from 18 to 62 years (M = 24.8, SD = 9.16); 117 identified as female, 29 as male, 2 as transgender, 1 as other, 2 preferred not to say.
Participants were ethnically diverse with 55 identifying as Hispanic or Latina/o, 52 as White, 30 as Black or African American, 22 as Asian, 5 as Other.

When asked their employment status, 48 were employed part-time, 23 were employed full-time, 17 were unemployed and looking for work, 7 were self-employed, 5 were graduate students, 1 was in the military, 1 was unable to work, and 49 were undergraduate students.
Ninety-one had completed some college or a two-year degree, 29 had completed college, 18 had a high school diploma, 12 had a professional degree, and 1 had a doctorate.
See also "Supplemental Material: Demographic Information for the Subset of Participants Who Completed Time 2 (n = 144)."
Flow of Expected Routines to Sampled Behavior and Retrospective Reports Panel A. Time 1 Routine Expectations and Time 2 Sampled Occasions
Expected Routine Content.

Using an online survey, 207 participants separately reported the person (who?), action (what?), and setting (where?) they expected to be typical of their weekly routines for 16 one-hour periods per day, from 7 AM to 11 PM, across all 7 days of the week (when?
; 112 time periods total).
This resulted in 18,736 time-period reports.
Participants were encouraged to consult their planners to increase the accuracy of their reported routines.

Instructions indicated that participants should report what they would 'normally be doing as part of [their] weekly routine,' including multiple activities within a given one-hour period and any known recurring alternatives (e.g., 'On Wednesdays from 5 to 6 PM, I am usually at work and then the gym, except on the last Wednesday of the month, when I skip the gym and go to happy hour instead').
They were also instructed to indicate when they did not expect a routine for a particular one-hour period by writing 'varies.'
Notably, Time 1 measured generalized expectations for recurring time periods rather than predictions for particular future dates.
For exact instructions, see Supplemental Material S5.
Expected Typicality.

For each time period, participants also rated the expected typicality of the described routine-i.e., how "likely it was to happen every week at the same time, place, and with the same people"-from 1 (Very Atypical) to 7 (Very Typical).
Next, 144 participants completed an experience-sampling phase lasting 10 to 14 days.
Data collection occurred at different calendar times across 10 recruitment waves, with 3 to 28 participants per wave (see Supplemental Material S6).
On average, experience sampling began 3.63 days after Time 1 (SD = 2.73, mode = 2, range = 0-11).
During this phase, participants received 3-4 text messages per day at the beginning of an hour between 8 AM and 11 PM asking about their current behavior.
The sampling window comprised the interval during which most offenses occurred in one archival sample of Canadian and U.S. cases involving alibi evidence (see Burke & Marion, 2012).
text.formatted: The sampling window comprised the interval during which most offenses occurred in one archival sample of Canadian and U.S. cases involving alibi evidence (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Burke & Marion, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For each message, participants were prompted to respond with 1) who they were with, 2) what they were doing, and 3) where they were, along with filler items about their current emotional state.
To prevent rehearsal of their responses, participants were instructed to avoid discussing their messages and to delete them.
If they could not respond within 45 minutes of receiving the message for whatever reason, they were asked to respond "defer."
On average, each participant provided 28.5 concurrent reports (SD = 8.27, range = 7-51).
After exclusions (discussed below), we retained 3,510 sampled occasions which averaged 24.38 eligible reports per participant.
Selection of Sampled Occasions.

Finally, just over a week later (M = 7.94 days, SD = 3.55: range: 1.77-35), 134 participants completed a personalized free-recall memory test asking them to recall their behavior during four occasions sampled at Time 2.

For each participant, the source-study researchers selected two occasions on which sampled behavior had been mostly or completely consistent with the expected routine reported at Time 1 and two on which it had been mostly or completely inconsistent, prioritizing completely consistent and completely inconsistent occasions (see Expectation-Behavior Consistency under Measures).
Retrospective Recall Task.
Participants were asked to imagine themselves as suspects in a criminal investigation and that the accuracy of their memory reports would serve as alibis supporting their innocence.
Study 1 participants reported alibis remotely via a Qualtrics survey, whereas Study 2 participants reported alibis in the laboratory during an interview with a trained RA.

To assist retrieval, participants first recalled a four-hour window (8:30 AM to 12:30 PM) containing the sampled one-hour window (e.g., 10 AM to 11 AM), before reporting their alibi for the target one-hour window.
Instructions emphasized that participants should not rely on any external memory aids and that they should avoid guessing.
For two of four sampled occasions, participants were cued only by the target one-hour window; for the other two sampled occasions, recall was elicited via a mental reinstatement of context procedure.
This elicitation technique manipulation had no significant effect on recall accuracy (see Measures for how this was coded) in Cárdenas et al. (2021) and was not of interest in the current work.
text.formatted: This elicitation technique manipulation had no significant effect on recall accuracy (see Measures for how this was coded) in <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cárdenas et al. (2021)</ref> and was not of interest in the current work.

text.text: Nonetheless, consistent with our preregistration we account for it statistically in our confirmatory model (described below).
In total, participants provided 507 retrospective reports: 111 participants provided four reports, 17 provided three, and six provided two; none provided only one.

Additionally, participants also reported on the quality of their memories and, in Study 1 only, indicated the frequency with which they used a daily planner to manage their schedules, and how often they had rehearsed their memories for the sampled occasions by looking at the text messages they had sent the researchers, as well as additional exploratory measures.
For planner-use and event-rehearsal results, see Supplemental Materials S12-S15.
Only Study 2 participants participated in Time 4 tasks.
After Time 3, they were instructed to search for evidence to corroborate their alibis.
Just over a week later (M = 8.42 days, SD = 1.48: range 7-13), they then provided a second retrospective report of their Time 2 activities for the same four sampled occasions via an online survey.
Participants provided a total of 218 additional retrospective reports: 49 participants provided four reports, four provided three, and five provided two; none provided only one.

Finally, participants answered additional questions completed by Study 1 participants at Time 3 (e.g., on their use of planners), as well as a novel question "Compared to your usual routine, how common was the above event?"
(1 = very uncommon to7 = very common).
Expectation-Behavior Consistency.
To assess expectation-behavior consistency, Cárdenas and colleagues (2021) compared each expected routine reported at Time 1 with behavior reported on the corresponding sampled occasion at Time 2.

Pairs of trained research assistants coded whether domain-level content-i.e., details about person, action, and settingmatched across the two reports (0 = no,1 = yes); one of the original authors resolved disagreements.

When participants reported multiple expected people, actions, or settings within a time period, a Time 2 sampled detail was coded as consistent if it matched any corresponding Time 1 detail reported for that domain and period.
The authors summed the three domain-level codes to produce an expectation-behavior consistency score ranging from 0 to 3 for each sampled occasion.
Higher scores indicated that sampled behavior matched the expected routine across more domains.

A mismatch therefore indicates that the expected routine did not describe behavior on the sampled occasion; it cannot establish whether participants could have anticipated a onetime disruption or whether the same time period would have matched on another week.
Interrater reliability across coder pairs ranged from αs = .78 to .90.
For coding instructions, see http://osf.io/abf4t/  (Holliday, 2003; Strange et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For coding instructions, see <ref type="url" target="http://osf.io/abf4t/">osf.io/abf4t/</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Holliday, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Strange et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For examples, see Supplemental Material S16.
Recall Accuracy.

To assess recall accuracy, Cárdenas and colleagues (2021) compared participants' retrospective reports at Time 3 and Time 4 with their Time 2 concurrent reports of behavior using the same person, action, and setting coding scheme.
text.formatted: To assess recall accuracy, <ref type="bibr">Cárdenas and colleagues (2021)</ref> compared participants' retrospective reports at Time 3 and Time 4 with their Time 2 concurrent reports of behavior using the same person, action, and setting coding scheme.

text.text: The authors summed the three domain-level codes to produce separate occasion-level accuracy scores for T2-T3 consistency and T2-T4 consistency, each ranging from 0 to 3.
Higher scores indicated greater occasion-level consistency between what participants had actually been doing and what they retrospectively reported doing.

Our preregistered analyses focus on T2-T3 recall accuracy because Time 4 reports followed an earlier retrieval attempt and an opportunity to seek corroborating evidence, complicating the interpretation of T2-T4 accuracy.
Only Study 2 included domain-level schema-reliance codes.
We operationalized schema reliance as a Time 3 or Time 4 report that matched the corresponding Time 1 expected routine.
Eligibility of Sampled Occasions.

Concurrent reports at Time 2 were excluded if during Time 1 prospective reporting, the participant had indicated no routine or, less commonly, a partial routine, as no measure of expectation-behavior consistency could be calculated (k = 348 observations).

We excluded another 1,694 reports because participants responded outside the specified 45-minute interval, indicated that they could not provide the requested information, or encountered technical or procedural problems that prevented them from receiving prompts.
See Supplemental Material S2 for details on exclusion reasons.
Supplemental Materials S7-S9 describe additional characteristics and the distributions of attempted sampling prompts and retained sampled occasions across time periods.
Supplemental Materials S10-S11 show that excluded and retained Time 2 observations had similar Time 1 expected-typicality ratings and temporal characteristics.
Source studies were completed by Spring 2018, before the widespread availability of large language models for survey completion had become a concern.
Therefore, they did not include AI-specific procedures to prevent participants from submitting LLMgenerated responses.

Due to technical errors during data collection in the source studies (e.g., an interviewer accidentally asking about a one-hour window that had not been sampled), recall accuracy could not be calculated for 29 of 536 retrospective reports.

Additionally, technical errors prevented an expectation-behavior consistency score from being calculated for an additional 21 retrospective reports (e.g., at Time 3, the interviewer accidentally asked about a sampled occasion corresponding to a Time 1 period with no specific expected routine).
We retained these reports because expected typicality and recall accuracy were available, and an expectation-behavior consistency score was not required for all preregistered analyses.
See Supplemental Material S2.
We report expected routines at the time-period and domain levels, and expectationbehavior consistency at the sampled-occasion and domain levels.
Time-period-and sampledoccasion-level results aggregate across the person, action, and setting domains; domain-level results show each domain separately.
Time-Period Level.
Across 18,736 time-period reports covering 7 AM to 11 PM, 207 participants reported a complete expected routine across the person, action, and setting domains for 92.83% of periods (k = 17,392).
They reported an expected routine for two of the three domains for 2.51% (k = 470), for only one domain for 1.13% (k = 212), and no routine for any domain for 3.53% (k = 662) of time periods.
At the domain level, participants reported routine expectations for the person, action, and setting domains in 96.29%, 93.50%, and 94.83% of time periods, respectively.
Expected typicality ratings were also high, M = 6.26 (Mdn = 7, SD = 1.16).
Most time periods (77.92%; k = 14,600) were rated as highly typical (6 or 7), whereas only 1.56% (k = 292) were rated as highly atypical (1 or 2).
Thus, people believed they had highly typical routines for nearly all queried time periods which excluded regular sleeping hours (11 PM to 7 AM).

Exploratory descriptive analyses show that although expected typicality ratings were generally high, this tendency did not characterize all participants to the same degree: nearly one third (29.95%; n = 62) had a mean rating below 6 (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Exploratory descriptive analyses show that although expected typicality ratings were generally high, this tendency did not characterize all participants to the same degree: nearly one third (29.95%; n = 62) had a mean rating below 6 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: High mean typicality ratings were broadly similar across participant characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, education, and employment status) and time-period characteristics (time of day and day of week; Supplemental Material S19).
Results reported here are similar among participants who completed the Time 1 reporting task (155) and those who did not (52; see Supplemental Materials S17-S18).
Sampled-Occasion Level.

Among the 2,665 of 3,510 (75.93%) sampled occasions corresponding to time periods previously rated as highly typical (6 or 7) at Time 1, sampled behavior matched an average of 1.36 of the three domains (SD = 1.01, Mdn = 1).

Of these sampled occasions, 24.02% (k = 640) did not match the expected routine in any domain, 31.59% (k = 842) matched one domain, 29.19% (k = 778) matched two domains, and 15.20% (k = 405) matched all three domains.
Thus, 44.39% of sampled occasions matched expectations across at least two of the three domains.
Figure 3, Panel A compares the number of expected routine domains with the number matched by sampled behavior.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>, Panel A compares the number of expected routine domains with the number matched by sampled behavior.

text.text: Similarly, when examining each domain separately, of 2,665 sampled occasions with high expected-typicality ratings, 51.18% (1,364) matched the expected person, 55.35% (1,475) matched the expected setting, and 29.04% (774) matched the expected action.
Descriptively, participants were less consistent about what they would be doing than who or where they would be with.
For a comparison of expected routines and the number that matched sampled behaviors within each domain, see Figure 3, Panel B.
text.formatted: For a comparison of expected routines and the number that matched sampled behaviors within each domain, see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>, Panel B.

text.text: Thus, even when participants rated their routines as highly typical, sampled behavior was often consistent with expectations in only some domains or none.
The degree to which expected routines matched sampled behavior also varied across and within participants ( Figure 4).
text.formatted: The degree to which expected routines matched sampled behavior also varied across and within participants ( Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>).

text.text: Exploratory analyses show that sampled behavior matched fewer expected domains among periods expected to be low to moderately typical (see Supplemental Material S20).
Low expectation-behavior consistency was also common across all time-period characteristics, albeit lower for action information, Sundays, evenings, and afternoons (see Figures S21-S22).
text.formatted: Low expectation-behavior consistency was also common across all time-period characteristics, albeit lower for action information, Sundays, evenings, and afternoons (see Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">S21-S22</ref>).

Panel B shows these percentages separately for each domain.

Next, we assessed whether higher expected typicality ratings predicted greater expectation-behavior consistency.
We fit a linear mixed-effects model predicting expectation-behavior consistency from expected typicality reported at Time 1.
Per our preregistration, we included random intercepts for participants, recruitment wave (1-10), and time periods (95 dayand-hour combinations) to account for nesting.
See Table 1.

text.text: Here, we asked how often later reports repeated an expected detail that had not matched sampled behavior and whether people were more likely to do so when they had rated the routine as more typical.
To answer these questions, we restricted the analysis to person, action, or setting domains in which the Time 1 expected detail differed from the Time 2 sampled detail.
This allowed occasions with one or more mismatching details to contribute only the relevant domains.
We coded schema reliance when the Time 3 retrospective report matched the Time 1 expectation within one of those domains.
Because the original authors did not code Time 1-Time 3 consistency in Study 1, this analysis includes only Study 2 data.
The analytic sample contained 328 domain-level observations from 126 sampled occasions reported by 59 participants.
Descriptively, participants showed schema reliance for 33.84% (111 of 328) of these expectation-inconsistent domain-level observations.
We fit a mixed-effects logistic regression predicting schema reliance (T1-T3 consistency) from expected typicality (1 to 7) while adjusting for domain type (person, action, setting).
A random intercept for sampled occasion accounted for multiple domain-level observations from the same occasion unique to each participant (e.g., Tuesday, 1 to 2 PM for JJID 101; 126 total).
Higher expected typicality predicted greater schema reliance, b = 1.13, SE = 0.34, z = 3.34, p < .001, OR = 3.08, 95% CI [1.59, 5.96].

text.text: Each one-point increase in expected typicality was associated with approximately three times greater odds of schema reliance.
Adding interactions between expected typicality and domain type did not improve model fit, χ²(2) = 0.64, p = .724.
Thus, the association did not reliably differ across person, action, and setting domains (see Supplemental Material S30).

When previously engaged in expectation-consistent behaviors, expectations about one's routines can help people reconstruct the past (e.g., Leins & Charman, 2016).
text.formatted: When previously engaged in expectation-consistent behaviors, expectations about one's routines can help people reconstruct the past (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Leins & Charman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, we show that behavior matches time-specific routine expectations much less often than people assume.

Regardless of participant-and time-period-level characteristics, participants reported expected routines for nearly all queried periods across all domains and rated most as highly typical, yet sampled occasions-particularly people's actions-infrequently unfolded as expected.
Subjective ratings of expected typicality weakly predicted expectation-behavior consistency.
When expectations differed from the sampled behavior, higher expected typicality predicted greater inaccurate reliance on routine knowledge in retrospective reports.
Together, these results suggest that routine expectations may make what would usually have happened seem plausible even when they do not describe the sampled occasion.

These results are consistent with metacognitive accounts of autobiographical belief and empirical research suggesting that, when direct recollection is difficult, people sometimes report their expected behaviors for that period rather than what they were actually doing (Charman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These results are consistent with metacognitive accounts of autobiographical belief and empirical research suggesting that, when direct recollection is difficult, people sometimes report their expected behaviors for that period rather than what they were actually doing <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Charman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This phenomenon may be especially consequential in criminal investigations, where innocent suspects must account for their behavior during a specified period on a particular past date (Crozier et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This phenomenon may be especially consequential in criminal investigations, where innocent suspects must account for their behavior during a specified period on a particular past date <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crozier et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Relying on what one usually does may seem reasonable as it can produce a broadly plausible and accurate account when behavior during that period had been expectation-consistent.
The current work suggests, however, that such reliance can mislead because innocent suspects may overestimate how reliably their usual behaviors occur at expected times.
Reports based on confident reliance on expectations of routine may therefore systematically bias alibis toward providing expectation-consistent, but inaccurate details.
Several limitations warrant consideration.

First, our analyses concern what participants ultimately reported and cannot rule out whether routine knowledge sometimes helped them remember what actually happened when an occasion deviated from the routine.

Second, because the sample included many students, the findings may not generalize to adults with different work, family, and recreational routines, although the student sample came from an urban commuter campus and most participants worked at least part time.
Third, we did not sample the same time period for each participant across multiple weeks.
Our findings therefore show how often routine expectations matched sampled occasions, not how often participants followed each routine over time.
Fourth, some sampled occasions lacked usable concurrent reports at Time 2, raising concern that report availability may have depended on what participants were doing.

Somewhat lessening this concern, excluded and retained periods had similar Time 1 expected-typicality ratings and occurred on similar weekdays and at similar times of day (see Supplemental Materials S10-S11).
However, if activities that deviated from expected routines were less likely to yield usable reports, retained observations may overstate how often sampled behavior was consistent with expectations.
Yet routine activities such as sleeping, working, or attending class could also impede responding, leaving the direction and magnitude of any selection bias unclear.
Fifth, real-time reporting may have made sampled occasions more memorable.

However, prior work suggests minimal effects of such reporting on memory (Thompson, 1982), participants recalled only four of approximately 28 sampled occasions, and controlling for selfreported event rehearsal did not substantively change the present results.
text.formatted: However, prior work suggests minimal effects of such reporting on memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Thompson, 1982)</ref>, participants recalled only four of approximately 28 sampled occasions, and controlling for selfreported event rehearsal did not substantively change the present results.

text.text: Finally, reporting routines across an entire week of time periods was demanding and may have encouraged loweffort responses.
This concern is reduced, though not eliminated, by supplemental analyses.

Time 1 expected-typicality ratings showed modest correspondence with Time 4 commonness ratings, and participants often reproduced the same expected details across reports (see Supplemental Materials S31-32).
Even participants who did not complete the full Time 1 routinereporting task described their lives as highly routine.
Therefore, non-completion was unlikely to indicate disengagement resulting from having either unusually many routines to report or unusually few.
Future work should better distinguish between misattribution errors in prospective reports of expected routines and retrospective reports (Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023).
text.formatted: Future work should better distinguish between misattribution errors in prospective reports of expected routines and retrospective reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In prospective reports, participants may have described real routines that occur at a different time than the one queried or only at a broader temporal scale (e.g., "in the morning" rather than 9-10 AM).
In retrospective reports, they may have reported real events-routine or not-that occurred outside the target interval.

These possibilities are consistent with time-slice errors, such as choosing the correct day but wrong week or the correct hour but wrong day (Laliberte et al., 2021), and telescoping errors in which events from outside a reporting interval are misdated as occurring within it (Neter & Waksberg, 1964; Rubin & Baddeley, 1989).
text.formatted: These possibilities are consistent with time-slice errors, such as choosing the correct day but wrong week or the correct hour but wrong day <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Laliberte et al., 2021)</ref>, and telescoping errors in which events from outside a reporting interval are misdated as occurring within it <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Neter & Waksberg, 1964;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Rubin & Baddeley, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Regardless of when the errors arose, routine-based inference may still be a poor guide to what happened during a particular occasion.
Future studies could repeatedly sample the same time periods to estimate how consistently individual routines recur.

Experiments could also manipulate the strength of a timespecific routine while holding a routine-inconsistent event constant, testing whether stronger routines improve memory for deviations or instead increase schema-consistent recall errors.
The current work suggests that people may be more confident in their knowledge of their routines than is warranted by their behavior on sampled occasions.
Higher expected typicality did not improve retrospective recall accuracy; when sampled behavior deviated from expectations, higher expected typicality instead predicted greater schema reliance.
Knowledge of one's routines may therefore provide a tempting basis for reconstructing the past.

Yet given how often behavior on sampled occasions diverged from expected routines, routine knowledge should be critically evaluated; otherwise, it may prematurely end the search for episode-specific details and lead people to report an inference as though it were a memory.

text.text: The research question, as written, is inconsistent with the analysis we preregistered we would perform.
The analysis does not account for the moderating effect of routine consistency (i.e., "typicality vs. atypicality of the events").
We retained the specified model as our primary model (reported in manuscript) and conducted an exploratory analysis examining whether routine consistency moderated this association.

We grouped relatively expectationinconsistent events (0-1 matching domains) and expectation-consistent events (2-3 matching domains), consistent with the criteria used to select the memory-test events and with the preregistration language.

""The manuscript describes 152 participants (80 in Study 1 and 72 in Study 2) as having completed Phase 1 (T1 -Expected Routines)."
However, when we reviewed all available Time 1 data, we found that 207, not 152, participants had consented and provided any Time 1 responses (i.e., completed one or more of the 112 time periods).
Cárdenas et al. reported the number of participants who "completed Phase 1" (p. 5).
As such, we failed to account for participants who provided some, but not all, Time 1 responses in our estimate.
However, In the supplemental materials, we report results of the smaller sample that completed Time 1 measures (112 time periods) and the complete sample.
These are substantively consistent.
"Results for Subset of Participants Who Completed Time 1 (n = 155)" and "Potential Effects of Attrition at Time 1".

Error After data acces s we retained data from these additional 55 participants because doing so was consistent with our preregistration: "We will use data available at each phase, such that responses to expectations about routine events (T1) will correspond to a larger sample size than responses to memory test (T3)."
Of these 207 participants, 155 reported on all 112 time periods at Time 1.
We recognize that 155 still differs from the 152 reported by Cárdenas et al.

We suspect that, by "completed," Cárdenas et al. meant that a participant had completed all 112 time periods and provided contact information, primarily a phone number, which was necessary for the Phase 2 experience sampling.
Of these 155 participants, only 151 reached the end of the Time 1 survey, where the demographic questions were located.
We cannot be completely certain why Cárdenas et al. reported that 152 rather than 151 participants completed Time 1.
The only variables omitted from the available Time 1 data concern participants' contact information, which was requested on the same page as the demographic questions.
It is possible that 152 participants provided contact information and that this criterion determined who Cárdenas et al. counted as having completed Time 1.
In summary: • 155 participants reported on all 112 time periods.
• 151 participants provided demographic information.
• The source study reported that 152 participants completed Time 1; one additional participant may have provided contact information but not demographic information.

Descriptively, demographic information did not differ among the subset of participants who later contributed Time 2 data (n = 144), ages ranged from 18 to 59 years (M = 24.18, SD = 8.27).
Of these participants, 110 identified as female, 27 as male, 2 as transgender, 1 as other, and 2 preferred not to say.

With respect to education, 71 reported some college, 29 had completed a 4-year degree, 17 were high school graduates, 14 had completed a 2-year degree, and 11 had a professional degree.

In main analyses we report data from any participants who reported prospective routines (or lack thereof) for at least one time period (N = 207).
Of those, 155 (75%) reported on potential routines for 100% of 112 time periods queried.
The number of time periods from this subset of participants was 17,360.
Results concerning expected routines and expected typicality for this smaller subset were consistent with those reported in the manuscript for the full sample.
Across 17,360 time periods, participants reported a full expected routine across the person, action, and setting domains for 92.40% (k = 16,041) and no expected routine for 3.73% (k = 647).

Expectedtypicality ratings were high on average (M = 6.26, Mdn = 7, SD = 1.14): participants rated 77.94% (k = 13,531) of time periods as highly typical (6 or 7) and 1.47% (k = 255) as highly atypical (1 or 2).
At Time 1, 155 of 207 participants reported whether they expected routine events for all 112 queried time periods.
The remaining 52 participants provided partial prospective reports, most often discontinuing after completing the Monday time periods (36 of 52 participants).
We compared completers and non-completers on the measures most important to the current work.
Both groups described their lives as highly routine.

Non-completers reported information for an average of 2.96 of the 3 routine domain levels (i.e., person, action, setting) per time period (SD = 0.32, Mdn = 3), compared with 2.84 among completers (SD = 0.62, Mdn = 3), a small difference, d = 0.20 [0.15, 0.26].
Expected typicality ratings were also highly similar across groups.
Non-completers' average expected typicality rating was 6.19 out of 7 (SD = 1.30, Mdn = 7), compared with 6.26 among completers (SD = 1.14, Mdn = 7), d = 0.06 [0.00, 0.11].

These comparisons likely somewhat overestimate non-completers' expected routines because task progress was confounded with day of week: participants completed the planner in Monday-to-Sunday order, and Monday-Thursday periods tended to receive slightly higher typicality ratings than Friday-Sunday periods (see S19).
We also examined whether task progress (0 to 100%) was associated with the average number of routine domain information reported per event (0 to 3) or with expected typicality (1 to 7).
Task progress refers to a Qualtrics-generated measure of the extent of progress a survey taker made before discontinuing a survey.

Task progress showed a very small negative association with routine domain information, b = -0.002, SE < 0.001, t(225.50) = -2.20, p = .029, such that each 10-percentage-point increase in survey completion corresponded to a negligible 0.02 fewer routine domains on the 0 to 3 scale.

text.text: Of note, this result did not meet our preregistered alpha level of .01.
Task progress was not associated with expected typicality, b = 0.001, SE = 0.002, t(216.10) = 0.70, p = .483.
In sum, the tendency to describe life as highly routine was not limited to participants who completed all Time 1 reports.
When people expect a time period to be low to moderately routine, how often does their actual behavior align with their expectation?

Among the 764 of 3,510 experience-sampled events that participants had rated as low to moderately typical (1 to 5) at Time 1, even fewer events occurred as expected than among events rated as highly typical.
Only 9.82% (k = 75) events were completely consistent with prospectively expected routines across all three coded domains, and 25% (k = 191) were consistent across two of three domains.
In contrast, 37.04 (k = 283) matched across only one domain, and 28.14% (k = 215) did not match any domain.

Because the model predicting expectation-behavior consistency showed that residual normality was violated, we fit our data to a cumulative link mixed model accounting for the ordinal structure of the data.
This ordinal robustness check produced the same conclusion as the primary model.
Expected typicality again significantly predicted expectation-behavior consistency, b = 0.18, SE = 0.03, z = 5.21, p < .001.

Given the null finding for the effect of typicality on recall accuracy at the global level (when aggregating person, setting, action domain levels), we examined whether typicality influenced recall accuracy at the level of detail.
We fit a mixed-effects model predicting accuracy at the level of detail with a random intercept for participants.
This yielded a sample of 1521 pieces of domain-level information (from 507 alibis).
Once again, expected typicality did not predict accuracy of the retrospective report, b = 0.02, SE = 0.01, t(868.40) = 1.33, p = .183.

There was a main effect of domain type: tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons showed that person details were recalled more accurately than action details, p < .001, and setting details were recalled more accurately than action details, p < .001, whereas person and setting details did not differ, p = .607.
