Were participants' beliefs about the routine nature of their life consistent across time?

To answer this question we examined objective and subjective sources of information, including the degree to which participants reproduced similar domain information (across person, setting, and action domains) across time and the consistency between their prospective and retrospective reports of expected typicality.
First, we found that participants often reiterated the same expected detail over time.

To directly test whether their routine-based reports were similar across time, we isolated cases where participants' original routine was wrong and then asked whether they repeated that same wrong detail later.

To examine this, we identified cases in which a detail (person, setting, action) participants expected at Time 1 did not match what actually occurred at Time 2 and was also reported inaccurately at Time 3.
We then asked whether the inaccurate Time 3 detail nevertheless matched the original Time 1 expectation.
1 It did in 43.7% of cases (87 of 199), indicating that even when participants were wrong, they still reproduced an expectationconsistent detail nearly half the time.
This tendency was similar for person-level information (49.1%) and setting-level information (48.5%), and somewhat lower for action-level information (35.1%).
At the alibi level, 52% of inaccurate reports about sampled occasions that matched expectations in no domains nevertheless included at least one detail from the participant's expected routine.
At Time 4, participants continued to make expectation-consistent errors in 37.3% of cases (69 of 185), suggesting continued, though reduced, reliance on schemas.
Second, we examined the consistency of perceived routineness at a more subjective level at Time 1 and at Time 4.
Two caveats apply to this analysis.

In our preregistration, we specified a mixed-effects model predicting recall accuracy (0-3) for 507 alibis from expected typicality ratings, controlling for recall method and including random intercepts for study and participants.
The study-level random intercept produced a singular fit and contributed less than .001 variance, so it was removed from the final model.
Here, we report the more parsimonious model without the covariate to show that the results were substantively unchanged.

Notably, although this

We note in the limitations that the source studies deliberately selected Time 3 occasions that overrepresented complete matches and mismatches between expected routines and sampled behavior (i.e., expectation-behavior consistency scores of 0 and 3).
This offered unambiguous within-participant examples in which routine knowledge was either an accurate or misleading basis for reconstruction.
However, partially matching occasions, although more common during experience sampling, were underrepresented.
Consequently, the present analyses offer limited evidence about whether expected typicality predicts recall accuracy for partially expectation-consistent occasions.

This limitation raises the possibility that the overall association between expected typicality (1 to 7) and recall accuracy (0 to 3) may not capture associations within relatively expectation-consistent and expectation-inconsistent events.
To formally examine this possibility, we conducted an exploratory moderation analysis.
While considering this analysis, we noticed an inconsistency in our preregistration materials, which we now report as Item 3 in our preregistration deviations disclosure table .

Our preregistered research question referred to a potential moderating effect of expectationbehavior consistency on the association between expected typicality and recall accuracy (i.e., "How well do ratings of expected typicality of behaviors predict accuracy of recall for typical vs.
atypical events?"), but the model code specified for this question tested only the overall association between expected typicality and recall accuracy (i.e., Recall Accuracy ~ Expected Typicality).
That is, the code did not include the moderating effect of expectation-behavior consistency.

For transparency, we conducted an exploratory moderation analysis in which we grouped relatively routine-inconsistent events (scores of 0 or 1) and expectation-consistent events (scores of 2 or 3), consistent with the criteria used to select the memory-test events in the source studies and the language of the preregistration.
The exploratory moderation analysis yielded substantively similar conclusions to the primary analysis.
The interaction between expected typicality and expectation-behavior consistency did not meet our preregistered alpha criterion of .01, b = 0.22, SE = 0.09, t(461.26) = 2.38, p = .018.

Expected typicality did not reliably predict accuracy for relatively expectationinconsistent events, b = -0.08, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.05], p = .241, or relatively expectation-consistent events, b = 0.14, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [0.004, 0.28], p = .043.

At Time 1, participants rated how typical each expected event was of their routine (1 = very atypical,7 = very typical), whereas at Time 4 they rated how common the reported event was compared with their usual routine (1 = very uncommon,7 = very common).
Second, only Study 2 participants completed the Time 4 commonness rating.
For a more direct comparison, we first report on expected typicality at Time 1 among only the subset of time periods queried at Time 3 in Study 2 (k = 226 versus the entire corpus of 18,736 periods).
Expected typicality at Time 1 was high (M = 6.27, Mdn = 7, SD = 1.02), with 77.43% (175 of 226) rated 6 or 7.
Time 4 commonness ratings were lower (M = 5.35, Mdn = 6, SD = 1.74), with 55.31% (125 of 226) rated 6 or 7.
However, this difference in typicality is not especially surprising because half of the Time 2 events were intentionally selected because they highly deviates from participants' routine expectations.
The more notable question is why this proportion was not lower.

One possibility is that participants relied on routine-based schemas when retrospectively reporting even schema-inconsistent events, consistent with prior work showing that people use routine knowledge to reconstruct the past (Cárdenas et al., 2021; Eastwood et al., 2021; Leins et al., 2016).

text.text: Thus, the present findings suggest that people may overestimate the routineness of their behavior both prospectively and retrospectively.
We then formally tested whether participants' Time 4 commonness ratings were related to their original Time 1 typicality ratings.

Accounting for by-participant variation, a mixed-effects model with random intercepts for participants indicated a small but significant positive association between Time 4 commonness and Time 1 typicality ratings, b = 0.10, SE = 0.04, t(223.35) = 2.62, p = .009.

Still, the persistence of relatively high Time 4 commonness ratings suggests that participants revised their routine judgments only partially, even after reporting on events that were often selected because they contradicted their original expectations.
